pos: n. and adj. (one holding the Reformed doctrines of grace; named for John Calvin, 1509–1564)
etymology: From Calvin, the Genevan Reformer, with the party suffix. Calvin himself never used it; it began as an opponents' label and was adopted, as most such names are, by the people it was aimed at.
biblical_def: In modern usage a Calvinist holds the Reformed soteriology summarised in five points: total depravity, unconditional election, particular redemption, effectual grace, and the perseverance of the saints. The texts it rests on are plain: “it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16); “as many as were ordained to eternal life believed” (Act 13:48); “All that the Father giveth me shall come to me” (John 6:37); “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44); “he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph 1:4). Strictly the word names a far wider system — covenant, worship, church order, the Christian life — of which the five points are one chapter.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Calvinist as a follower of Calvin; a person who embraces the theological doctrines of Calvin, and Calvinism as the doctrines relating to predestination, particular redemption, total depravity, effectual calling, and the perseverance of the saints.
webster_full: CALVINIST, n. A follower of Calvin; a person who embraces the theological doctrines of Calvin.

CALVINISM, n. The theological tenets or doctrines of Calvin and his followers. The peculiar doctrines of Calvin respect predestination, particular redemption, total depravity, effectual calling, and the perseverance of the saints.
scriptures: So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.
All that the Father giveth me shall come to me; and him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.
No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day.
According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:
For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?
corruption_summary: The five points are treated as the whole of the system, and the man they are named after would not have recognised a Christianity that stopped there.
corruption_paragraphs: The commonest corruption is a reduction. TULIP is a twentieth-century mnemonic summarising the Synod of Dort's answer to five specific Arminian articles — it was a reply to a set of objections, not a summary of the faith — and a man may hold all five and know nothing of the covenant, the sacraments, the law's third use, vocation, or the shape of worship. Calvin's own Institutes give more space to prayer than to predestination. A Christianity that consists of five points defended online is not Calvinism; it is a fragment of it, memorised.

The second corruption is temper, and it is the one that makes the doctrine hated. Paul's own handling of election ends in a doxology — O the depth of the riches both of the wisdom and knowledge of God — and his stated reaction to the lost is great heaviness and continual sorrow in his heart, with a wish that he himself were accursed for his brethren. Where the doctrine produces superiority instead of that, something has been learned wrongly, and 1 Corinthians 3:4 has the word for a party spirit that names itself after a teacher: carnal.

The label is also used loosely by both sides. Opponents use it to mean fatalism, which it is not: the same confession that teaches the decree teaches that it offers no violence to the will of the creature. Adherents use it as a badge of identity, which Calvin would have refused; he asked to be buried in an unmarked grave, and the tradition that bears his name has spent five centuries doing the opposite.
roots_summary: Greek eklego (G1586), to choose out; proorizo (G4309), to predestinate; tasso (G5021), to appoint, ordain; helko (G1670), to draw.
roots_lines: Greek eklego (G1586) — to choose out, elect; Ephesians 1:4, John 15:16, 1 Corinthians 1:27.
Greek proorizo (G4309) — to predestinate; Romans 8:29–30, Ephesians 1:5, 1:11.
Greek tasso (G5021) — to appoint, ordain; Acts 13:48; helko (G1670), to draw; John 6:44, 12:32.
usage: “Not of him that willeth… but of God that sheweth mercy” — the sentence the system is built on.
“As many as were ordained to eternal life believed” — the order of the two verbs.
“I am of Paul… are ye not carnal?” — Paul's word for a party named after a teacher.

pos: n. and adj. (one holding the system of Jacobus Arminius, 1560–1609; conditional election and resistible grace)
etymology: From Arminius, the Latinised name of Jakob Hermanszoon, professor at Leiden, whose followers set out five articles in the Remonstrance of 1610 — whence Remonstrant, the older name.
biblical_def: Arminianism affirms conditional election (God chooses those He foresaw would believe), a universal atonement, prevenient grace that is genuinely resistible, and, in most forms, the possibility of falling from grace. Its texts are real and must be answered: “God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son: that whosoever believeth in him should not perish” (John 3:16); God “will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth” (1Ti 2:4); Christ is “the propitiation… for the sins of the whole world” (1Jn 2:2); “whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate” (Rom 8:29). The Reformed reply turns on what foreknowledge means and on whom the all and the world denote.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines Arminian as one of a sect or party of Christians, so called from Arminius, who holds that God has not fixed the future state of mankind by an absolute unconditional decree, but determined to bestow salvation on those who believe and persevere.
webster_full: ARMINIAN, n. One of a sect or party of Christians, so called from Arminius, or Harmensen, of Holland.

ARMINIAN, a. Pertaining to the Arminians. The distinguishing tenets are: that God has not fixed the future state of mankind by an absolute unconditional decree; that Jesus Christ died for all men and not for the elect only; that man has power to do good works; and that grace is not irresistible.
scriptures: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life.
Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth.
And he is the propitiation for our sins: and not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.
For whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate to be conformed to the image of his Son, that he might be the firstborn among many brethren.
So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
corruption_summary: The name is used as an insult for anyone insufficiently precise, and it names a definite historical system that deserves to be answered rather than sneered at.
corruption_paragraphs: The word has become the Reformed world's general-purpose slur, applied to any believer who has not read Dort — which is most of the church, including a great many who would accept the doctrines of grace if anyone put them kindly. That usage is both uncharitable and imprecise. Arminianism is a defined system, set out in five articles in 1610 by men who were pastors and scholars, and it was answered article by article at Dort in a document that took months. A position worth a synod is worth an argument, and the man who can only produce the label has not made one.

The genuine difference is not over whether faith is required — both sides say it is — but over where faith comes from. The Reformed hold that it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8) and the fruit of a new birth that precedes it (John 1:13); the Arminian holds that prevenient grace restores the ability and the man decides. Everything else follows from that one question, including whether the decisive difference between the saved and the lost lies finally in God or in the man; and every honest conversation about the five points arrives there sooner or later.

The Reformed should also concede what the texts plainly say. God does declare that He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked; the offer of the gospel is universal, sincere, and to be pressed on every creature; and a hyper-Calvinism that will not freely invite sinners has departed further from Scripture than the Arminianism it despises. Ezekiel 33:11 and Romans 9:16 are both in the book, and a theology that can only hold one of them is not yet finished.
roots_summary: Greek proginosko (G4267), to foreknow; pas (G3956), all; kosmos (G2889), world; thelo (G2309), to will, desire.
roots_lines: Greek proginosko (G4267) — to foreknow; Romans 8:29, 11:2, 1 Peter 1:20 — of persons, not of facts about them.
Greek kosmos (G2889) — world; John 3:16, 1 John 2:2, and of the ordered system opposed to God, 1 John 2:15.
Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, desire; 1 Timothy 2:4, 2 Peter 3:9, Matthew 23:37.
usage: “Whom he did foreknow, he also did predestinate” — the verse the whole debate turns on.
“Who will have all men to be saved” — a text the Reformed must answer, not avoid.
“Not of him that willeth… but of God” — the answer, and it is a text too.

pos: n. and adj. (in theology, one holding that no office or authority in church or home is restricted by sex)
etymology: French égalitaire, from égal, equal. In evangelical usage the word names the position set against complementarianism; both terms date from the 1980s, though the dispute is older.
biblical_def: Egalitarianism holds that Scripture assigns no permanent functional distinction between men and women in church office or in marriage. Its central text is “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:28), read together with the women who plainly laboured in the apostolic churches — Phebe a servant of the church (Rom 16:1), Priscilla instructing Apollos (Act 18:26), Philip's four daughters which did prophesy (Act 21:9). The complementarian reply rests on the restriction and its stated ground: “I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man… For Adam was first formed, then Eve” (1Ti 2:12–13), and on “the head of the woman is the man” (1Co 11:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for egalitarian, the word being later than his dictionary; he defines equality as an agreement of things in dimensions, quantity, or quality; likeness; the same degree of dignity or claims.
webster_full: EQUALITY, n. An agreement of things in dimensions, quantity or quality; likeness; similarity in regard to two things compared.
2. The same degree of dignity or claims.
3. Evenness; uniformity; sameness in state or continued course.
4. Evenness; plainness; uniformity; as an equality of surface.
scriptures: There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus.
But I suffer not a woman to teach, nor to usurp authority over the man, but to be in silence.
For Adam was first formed, then Eve.
But I would have you know, that the head of every man is Christ; and the head of the woman is the man; and the head of Christ is God.
Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it;
And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly.
corruption_summary: Equality of worth and identity of role are treated as the same claim, and Galatians 3:28 answers the first question without addressing the second.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 3:28 is the hinge, and the context settles what it is arguing. Paul is not describing church order; he is concluding an argument about who may be justified by faith and inherit the promise made to Abraham — the verse ends ye are all one in Christ Jesus, and the next verse draws the conclusion: then are ye Abraham's seed, and heirs according to the promise. It abolishes every distinction as a ground of standing before God, and it does so in three pairs. If it abolished role along with standing, it would abolish the distinction between slave and free as thoroughly as that between male and female, and the same apostle goes on giving instructions to both.

The complementarian position stands or falls on the reason Paul attaches to the restriction. Had he grounded 1 Timothy 2:12 in the culture of Ephesus, or in the education of women, or in a local disorder, the restriction would expire with its cause; he grounds it instead in the order of creation — for Adam was first formed, then Eve — which does not expire, and in Genesis 2, which precedes the fall. That is why the argument cannot be settled by showing that women prophesied, served, taught other women, instructed Apollos privately, or carried the epistle to the Romans. All of that is in the text, and none of it is the office in question.

There is a corruption on the complementarian side, and it is uglier than the exegetical error it opposes. Ephesians 5 gives the husband a single verb repeated three times — love, as Christ loved the church and gave himself for it — and a headship defined by crucifixion. A man who quotes 1 Timothy 2 to secure his own comfort, who treats his wife's judgment as an obstacle rather than a gift, or who calls domination order, has taken the half of the doctrine that costs him nothing. The Bible's complementarianism is not a division of privileges; it is a division of sacrifices, and the heavier one falls on the head.
roots_summary: Greek arsen (G730) and thelu (G2338), male and female; authenteo (G831), to usurp authority; kephale (G2776), head; hupotasso (G5293), to submit.
roots_lines: Greek ouk eni arsen kai thelu (G730, G2338) — there is neither male nor female; Galatians 3:28.
Greek authenteo (G831) — to exercise or usurp authority over; 1 Timothy 2:12 only.
Greek kephale (G2776) — head; 1 Corinthians 11:3, Ephesians 5:23; hupotasso (G5293), Ephesians 5:22, 5:24, 1 Peter 3:1.
usage: “Neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” — three pairs, and a question about standing.
“For Adam was first formed, then Eve” — the reason given, and it precedes the fall.
“As Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it” — the half that costs the head everything.

pos: n. and adj. (one holding that the miraculous and revelatory gifts ceased with the apostolic age)
etymology: From Latin cessare, to cease. The position is older than the label, which is modern and was coined largely by its opponents.
biblical_def: Cessationism holds that the revelatory and sign gifts — apostleship in the New Testament sense, prophecy, tongues, and the attesting miracles — belonged to the foundation of the church and ceased with it. Its arguments are three. The foundation is laid once: the church is “built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone” (Eph 2:20). The signs authenticated the messengers: “the signs of an apostle were wrought among you” (2Co 12:12), and the word was “confirmed unto us by them that heard him; God also bearing them witness, both with signs and wonders” (Heb 2:3–4). And Paul dates the gifts' expiry: “whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease… when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away” (1Co 13:8–10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines cessation as a stopping; a rest; a ceasing or discontinuance, as of action or motion.
webster_full: CESSATION, n. A ceasing; a stop; a rest; the act of discontinuing motion or action of any kind.
2. A ceasing or suspension of the operation or effect of any thing.
3. Rest; a pause; a stop.
scriptures: And are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ himself being the chief corner stone;
Truly the signs of an apostle were wrought among you in all patience, in signs, and wonders, and mighty deeds.
How shall we escape, if we neglect so great salvation; which at the first began to be spoken by the Lord, and was confirmed unto us by them that heard him;
Charity never faileth: but whether there be prophecies, they shall fail; whether there be tongues, they shall cease; whether there be knowledge, it shall vanish away.
But when that which is perfect is come, then that which is in part shall be done away.
corruption_summary: Cessationism is stated as the belief that God no longer works miracles, which is not the position and would be easy to refute.
corruption_paragraphs: The position is regularly misreported, sometimes by its own advocates. Cessationism does not say that God has stopped healing, answering prayer, or acting providentially and extraordinarily; it says that a particular set of gifts, given to authenticate the apostolic message while the canon was being completed, ceased with the office they attended. A cessationist may pray for the sick with real expectation and believe every one of the miracles in Acts, and the caricature that he does not is answered by James 5, which he obeys.

The honest difficulty is 1 Corinthians 13:10 — the perfect that is to come. If it is the completed canon, the gifts ceased in the first century; if it is the return of Christ, they continue until then, and verse 12 makes that reading hard to dismiss, since face to face and known even as also I am known describe something more than a finished book. Many careful cessationists therefore rest their case on Ephesians 2:20 and the foundational nature of the office rather than on this text, and the argument is stronger for the concession.

The corruption in practice is a functional deism: a doctrine held so tightly that a congregation stops expecting God to do anything it has not scheduled. First Thessalonians 5:19–21 stands over that with three commands in a row — quench not the Spirit, despise not prophesyings, prove all things — and the middle one is as binding as the third. A church that has made itself immune to enthusiasm has usually paid for the immunity with expectancy.
roots_summary: Greek pauo (G3973), to cease; katargeo (G2673), to render inoperative, do away; teleios (G5046), perfect, complete; themelios (G2310), foundation.
roots_lines: Greek pauo (G3973) — to cease; 1 Corinthians 13:8, of tongues, in the middle voice.
Greek katargeo (G2673) — to be done away; 1 Corinthians 13:8, 13:10, of prophecy and knowledge.
Greek themelios (G2310) — foundation; Ephesians 2:20, 1 Corinthians 3:11, Hebrews 6:1.
usage: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” — a foundation is laid once.
“When that which is perfect is come” — the honest difficulty in the case.
“Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings” — three commands, and the middle one binds too.

pos: n. and adj. (one holding that all the spiritual gifts continue in the church until Christ returns)
etymology: From continue, Latin continuare. Like cessationist, a modern label for an old position; the older Reformed writers spoke instead of extraordinary and ordinary gifts.
biblical_def: Continuationism holds that no text withdraws the gifts, and that they remain available until the Lord returns. Its case: the gifts are distributed by the Spirit's present choice — “all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will” (1Co 12:11); they are commanded to be sought — “Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy” (1Co 14:1); they are not to be suppressed — “Quench not the Spirit. Despise not prophesyings. Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” (1Th 5:19–21); and Peter dates the outpouring to the whole last days: “it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh” (Act 2:17).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines continuation as extension or carrying on to a further point; the state of being continued; uninterrupted extension or succession.
webster_full: CONTINUATION, n. Extension of existence in a series or line; succession uninterrupted.
2. Extension or carrying on to a further point of time.
3. Extension in space; production; a carrying on in length.
scriptures: But all these worketh that one and the selfsame Spirit, dividing to every man severally as he will.
Follow after charity, and desire spiritual gifts, but rather that ye may prophesy.

And it shall come to pass in the last days, saith God, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh: and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, and your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams:
corruption_summary: The command to prove all things is dropped, and Paul gave it in the same breath as the command not to despise prophesyings.
corruption_paragraphs: First Thessalonians 5:19–21 is three commands and the movement most attached to the first two habitually loses the third. Quench not the Spirit; despise not prophesyings; prove all things; hold fast that which is good. Testing is not the cold alternative to openness; it is part of the same instruction, and Paul gives the church the duty of judging what is spoken: “let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge” (1Co 14:29). A prophecy that may not be examined is not a New Testament prophecy, whatever else it is.

The graver corruption is the claim of fresh revelation with the authority of Scripture — a word from the Lord that adds to, corrects, or overrides the text. Whatever the continuationist means by prophecy, it cannot be that; the canon is closed, and the sufficiency of Scripture is not a cessationist distinctive but a Reformation one. Where the gift is claimed and the claim carries binding authority, the effect is a second Bible with no gate on it, and the history of such movements is uniform.

The cessationist's mirror-error should be named in the same breath, since 1 Corinthians 14 was written to a church that had the gifts and used them badly, and Paul's remedy is regulation rather than abolition — two or three, in turn, with an interpreter, decently and in order. He does not tell them to stop; he tells them how. A church that has neither the disorder nor the power has solved the problem of 1 Corinthians 14 by a method the chapter never proposes.
roots_summary: Greek charisma (G5486), a gift of grace; pneumatikos (G4152), spiritual, of the gifts; sbennumi (G4570), to quench; dokimazo (G1381), to prove, test.
roots_lines: Greek charisma (G5486) — gift; Romans 12:6, 1 Corinthians 12:4, 12:9, 12:31, 1 Peter 4:10.
Greek sbennumi (G4570) — to quench; 1 Thessalonians 5:19, Ephesians 6:16, Matthew 12:20.
Greek dokimazo (G1381) — to prove, test; 1 Thessalonians 5:21, 1 John 4:1, Romans 12:2.
usage: “Dividing to every man severally as he will” — the Spirit's present choice.
“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good” — the third command in the same breath.
“Let the prophets speak two or three, and let the other judge” — regulation, not abolition.

pos: n. and adj. (one holding that the prophecies of Matthew 24 and much of Revelation were fulfilled in the first century)
etymology: Latin praeteritus, gone by, past. The school takes its name from where it locates the fulfilment: behind us.
biblical_def: Preterism holds that the Olivet discourse and much of Revelation were fulfilled in the events of AD 66–70, when Jerusalem fell and the temple was destroyed. Its two pillars are time-texts. The Lord said, “Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled” (Mat 24:34), having predicted of the temple, “There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down” (Mat 24:2); and Luke's version replaces the abomination with an army: “when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh” (Luk 21:20). Revelation twice states its own urgency: “things which must shortly come to pass” (Rev 1:1; Rev 22:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines preterite as past; gone by; applied to the tense in grammar which expresses an action or being perfectly past or finished.
webster_full: PRETERIT, a. Past; applied to the tense in grammar which expresses an action or being perfectly past or finished.
PRETERITION, n. The act of passing by; a passing over or omission.
scriptures: Verily I say unto you, This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled.
And Jesus said unto them, See ye not all these things? verily I say unto you, There shall not be left here one stone upon another, that shall not be thrown down.
And when ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies, then know that the desolation thereof is nigh.
The Revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave unto him, to shew unto his servants things which must shortly come to pass; and he sent and signified it by his angel unto his servant John:
And he said unto me, These sayings are faithful and true: and the Lord God of the holy prophets sent his angel to shew unto his servants the things which must shortly be done.
corruption_summary: Partial and full preterism are treated as one position, and the second denies a future bodily return and is outside the creeds.
corruption_paragraphs: The distinction that must be kept is between partial and full preterism. The partial preterist holds that Matthew 24 and much of Revelation were fulfilled in AD 70, and that the bodily return of Christ, the general resurrection and the last judgment remain future; that view is held by orthodox men across the Reformed tradition and is a question of interpretation. Full or consistent preterism holds that all prophecy, including the second coming and the resurrection, was fulfilled in the first century; that is not an interpretive variation but a denial of an article of the creed, and it puts its holders where Hymenaeus and Philetus stood, saying that the resurrection is past already (2Ti 2:18).

The strength of the position is that it takes the time-texts seriously, and its opponents often do not. This generation shall not pass is a difficulty for every futurist reading, and the attempts to make generation mean race, or the generation that sees the signs, are strained. Equally, the preterist has to account for language in the same discourse that has never plainly happened — the sun darkened, the powers of heaven shaken, the Son of man coming in the clouds with power and great glory — and the apocalyptic-imagery answer, though not unreasonable, has to be applied consistently or it becomes a way of dissolving whatever is inconvenient.

The pastoral corruption of every prophetic school is the same: a system so satisfying that it becomes the lens for the newspaper and eventually for the Bible. The Lord's own application of the discourse is not a chart but a posture — watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour — and any scheme, preterist or futurist, that leaves a man less watchful has failed the passage it claims to explain.
roots_summary: Greek genea (G1074), generation; en tachei (G5034), shortly, speedily; eggus (G1451), at hand, near; eremosis (G2050), desolation.
roots_lines: Greek genea (G1074) — generation; Matthew 24:34, 23:36, 12:39, Luke 21:32.
Greek en tachei (G5034) — shortly, speedily; Revelation 1:1, 22:6, Romans 16:20.
Greek eremosis (G2050) — desolation; Matthew 24:15, Luke 21:20, Daniel 9:27 in the Greek.
usage: “This generation shall not pass, till all these things be fulfilled” — the text every other school must answer.
“When ye shall see Jerusalem compassed with armies” — Luke's plainer version.
“Saying that the resurrection is past already” — where full preterism ends.

pos: n. and adj. (one holding that the bulk of unfulfilled prophecy awaits a still-future fulfilment)
etymology: From future, Latin futurus, about to be. The school is named, like preterism, for where it places the fulfilment.
biblical_def: Futurism holds that the greater part of Revelation, and often the latter half of the Olivet discourse, await fulfilment at the end of the age. Its texts are the plainly unfulfilled ones: “the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first” (1Th 4:16); “this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go” (Act 1:11); “the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise” (2Pe 3:10); “they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years” (Rev 20:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines future as that is to be or come hereafter; and futurity as time to come, the state of being yet to come, or the events which are yet to happen.
webster_full: FUTURE, a. That is to be or come hereafter; that will exist at any time after the present.
FUTURITY, n. Future time; time to come.
2. Event to come.
3. The state of being yet to come, or to happen.
scriptures: For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
Which also said, Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven? this same Jesus, which is taken up from you into heaven, shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go into heaven.

But the day of the Lord will come as a thief in the night; in the which the heavens shall pass away with a great noise, and the elements shall melt with fervent heat, the earth also and the works that are therein shall be burned up.

And I saw thrones, and they sat upon them, and judgment was given unto them: and I saw the souls of them that were beheaded for the witness of Jesus, and for the word of God, and which had not worshipped the beast, neither his image, neither had received his mark upon their foreheads, or in their hands; and they lived and reigned with Christ a thousand years.
But of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only.
corruption_summary: Prophecy is turned into a schedule, and the Lord attached the discourse to a day and hour no man knoweth.
corruption_paragraphs: The characteristic corruption of futurism is the chart. Once the bulk of prophecy is placed ahead, the temptation is to arrange it — a sequence, a timetable, an identification of the present decade with a chapter — and the last two centuries are littered with dated predictions that failed and took believers' credibility with them. Matthew 24:36 is the sentence the whole enterprise runs against: of that day and hour knoweth no man, no, not the angels of heaven, but my Father only. A scheme that produces a date has contradicted the passage it is built on.

The second corruption is escapism. Where the future is a catastrophe from which the church is to be extracted, cultural labour, political duty, long-term building and even evangelistic patience begin to look pointless — why polish the brass on a sinking ship. The New Testament draws the opposite inference from the same expectation: seeing that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness (2Pe 3:11), and the servant found watching is the one found working.

That said, the futurist holds something the church must not lose. There is a day appointed; there will be a shout, a trumpet, a resurrection of bodies, and a visible return of the same Jesus in the manner He went. A theology that has spiritualised all of it into a permanent present has kept the ethics and dropped the hope, and the ethics do not survive the loss for long.
roots_summary: Greek parousia (G3952), coming, presence; apokalupsis (G602), revealing; epiphaneia (G2015), appearing; salpigx (G4536), trumpet.
roots_lines: Greek parousia (G3952) — coming, arrival; Matthew 24:3, 24:27, 1 Thessalonians 4:15, James 5:7–8.
Greek epiphaneia (G2015) — appearing; 2 Thessalonians 2:8, 1 Timothy 6:14, Titus 2:13, 2 Timothy 4:8.
Greek salpigx (G4536) — trumpet; 1 Thessalonians 4:16, 1 Corinthians 15:52, Matthew 24:31.
usage: “Shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go” — bodily, visibly, the same Jesus.
“Of that day and hour knoweth no man” — the sentence every chart runs against.
“What manner of persons ought ye to be” — the inference Scripture draws from the end.

pos: adj. (bound by a written historic confession of faith)
etymology: From confession, Latin confiteri, to acknowledge, to say the same thing as another. A confession is the church saying back to God, and before men, what He has said.
biblical_def: A confessional church is one bound by a written historic confession — the Second London Confession of 1689, the Westminster Standards, the Heidelberg Catechism, the Three Forms of Unity. The practice is apostolic in principle. Paul hands Timothy a fixed deposit: “Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” (2Ti 1:13); he quotes what looks like an existing confession, “God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit…” (1Ti 3:16); he delivers a summary he had himself received (1Co 15:3–4); and Jude commands contending “for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints” (Jud 1:3) — a faith with content, deliverable and therefore statable.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines confession of faith as a summary of the articles of Christian faith, and confession as the acknowledgment of any thing, or the profession of belief.
webster_full: CONFESSION, n. The acknowledgment of a crime, fault or something to one's disadvantage; open declaration of guilt.
2. Avowal; the act of acknowledging.
3. The act of disclosing sins or faults to a priest.
4. A formulary in which the articles of faith are comprised; a creed to be assented to or signed.
scriptures: Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.

Beloved, when I gave all diligence to write unto you of the common salvation, it was needful for me to write unto you, and exhort you that ye should earnestly contend for the faith which was once delivered unto the saints.
For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;
That if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised him from the dead, thou shalt be saved.
corruption_summary: A confession is set against Scripture as though it competed, and every church that says no creed but the Bible has a creed and has declined to write it down.
corruption_paragraphs: The standing objection is that a confession adds to Scripture or rivals it. It does neither, and the confessions say so first: the Second London Confession opens by stating that the Holy Scripture is the only sufficient, certain and infallible rule of all saving knowledge, faith and obedience, and that the supreme judge in all controversies can be no other than the Holy Spirit speaking in the Scripture. A confession is a subordinate standard — a church's public answer to the question of what it understands the Bible to teach, offered so that it may be checked, argued with, and if necessary corrected by the Bible.

“No creed but the Bible” is itself a creed, and it has an unhappy record. Every congregation has a doctrine; the only question is whether it is written where a visitor can read it and a member can hold the elders to it, or whether it lives unrecorded in the pastor's head and changes with him. The unwritten creed is not more biblical, only less accountable. It is a notable historical fact that the churches which abandoned the confessions in the name of Scripture alone were, within two generations, the ones that lost the deity of Christ.

The corruption on the confessional side is real and is worth naming: subscription that has become a formality, doctrine held with precision and no warmth, and a church better at defending its confession than at obeying it. Paul's phrase guards against exactly that, because he does not merely say hold the form of sound words; he says hold it in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. A confession recited without those is a form of sound words and nothing else.
roots_summary: Greek homologeo (G3670), to confess, say the same thing; hupotuposis (G5296), a pattern, form, outline; paradidomi (G3860), to deliver, hand down; parathenke (G3866), a deposit.
roots_lines: Greek homologeo (G3670) — to confess; Romans 10:9, 1 John 1:9, 4:2, Hebrews 13:15.
Greek hupotuposis (G5296) — a form, pattern; 2 Timothy 1:13, 1 Timothy 1:16.
Greek parathenke (G3866) — that which is committed, a deposit; 1 Timothy 6:20, 2 Timothy 1:12, 1:14.
usage: “Hold fast the form of sound words” — a fixed deposit, handed on.
“The faith which was once delivered unto the saints” — a faith with content, and therefore statable.
“In faith and love which is in Christ Jesus” — the clause that keeps a confession from being a formality.

pos: adj. (of preaching, drawing the point of the sermon from the point of the text, usually through a book)
etymology: Latin exponere, to set forth, to lay open. An exposition lays the text open; the alternative, imposition, lays something over it.
biblical_def: Expositional preaching makes the point of the passage the point of the sermon. Its charter is the reading at the Water Gate: “So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” (Neh 8:8) — read, explain, apply. Paul's charge is the same: “Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine” (2Ti 4:2), and “give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13). Its ambition is Paul's at Ephesus: “I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27). The Lord Himself did it on the Emmaus road, “and beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself” (Luk 24:27).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines exposition as explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author, or of any passage or writing.
webster_full: EXPOSITION, n. A laying open; a setting to public view.
2. Explanation; interpretation; a laying open the sense or meaning of an author, or of any passage or writing.
EXPOSITOR, n. One who expounds or explains; an interpreter.
scriptures: So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading.
Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all longsuffering and doctrine.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God.
And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself.
corruption_summary: A running commentary is mistaken for exposition, and Nehemiah 8:8 requires that the sense be given and the people made to understand.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 8:8 contains three verbs and a church usually loses one of them. They read the book distinctly — the text itself, plainly; they gave the sense — explanation, the work of the study; and they caused the people to understand the reading — which is not the same as having explained it, and is where most preaching stops. A sermon that has read the passage and produced accurate observations about it has done two thirds of the job. Whether anyone in the room now understands is a separate question, and it is the one the verse makes decisive.

The counterfeit at the other extreme is the text as a doorway: a verse read, a topic entered, and the passage never seen again. That is imposition, not exposition, and its tell is that the sermon would be unchanged had a different verse been read. The discipline of preaching consecutively through books exists to prevent it, because a man working through a book must preach what comes next, including what he would not have chosen, and his congregation gets the whole counsel of God rather than the parts of it he finds congenial.

Expositors have their own besetting sin, and it is dryness that congratulates itself. Paul's charge in 2 Timothy 4:2 has doctrine in it and also reproof, rebuke, exhortation and all longsuffering, and Luke 24 ends not with a well-organised outline but with two men saying, did not our heart burn within us while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures. Opening the Scriptures is the method; a burning heart is the evidence it was done.
roots_summary: Greek diermeneuo (G1329), to expound, interpret; dianoigo (G1272), to open thoroughly; kerusso (G2784), to preach, herald; Hebrew parash (H6567), to make distinct; sekel (H7922), sense, understanding.
roots_lines: Hebrew parash (H6567) — distinctly, made plain; Nehemiah 8:8, Leviticus 24:12, Numbers 15:34.
Greek diermeneuo (G1329) — to expound, interpret; Luke 24:27, Acts 9:36, 1 Corinthians 12:30.
Greek kerusso (G2784) — to preach as a herald; 2 Timothy 4:2, Romans 10:14–15, Mark 16:15.
usage: “Gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading” — three verbs, and the third decides.
“I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” — the whole book, including what one would not choose.
“Did not our heart burn within us… while he opened to us the scriptures” — the evidence.

pos: n. (the resurgence of Reformed soteriology among younger evangelicals from the late 1990s)
etymology: So named by observers rather than adherents; also called the Young, Restless and Reformed movement after a 2006 book, and the resurgence.
biblical_def: New Calvinism names the recovery of the doctrines of grace among evangelicals who did not inherit them — largely outside the historic Reformed denominations, often Baptist or non-denominational, and gathered around conferences, publishers and a handful of preachers rather than around presbyteries. Its convictions are the old ones: “it is not of him that willeth… but of God that sheweth mercy” (Rom 9:16); “by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves” (Eph 2:8). Its besetting risk is the one Paul named at Corinth, where converts organised around teachers: “while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?” (1Co 3:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) has no entry for the movement, which is modern; his definition of Calvinism stands as the doctrinal content: predestination, particular redemption, total depravity, effectual calling, and the perseverance of the saints.
webster_full: CALVINISM, n. The theological tenets or doctrines of Calvin and his followers.
The peculiar doctrines of Calvin respect predestination, particular redemption, total depravity, effectual calling, and the perseverance of the saints.
scriptures: So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.
For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
For while one saith, I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos; are ye not carnal?
I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase.
For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears;
corruption_summary: A recovery of doctrine is mistaken for a recovery of churchmanship, and the movement's weakness has been everything the five points do not cover.
corruption_paragraphs: The resurgence recovered soteriology and largely left the rest — ecclesiology, confessional subscription, church discipline, the sacraments, the regulative principle, the Lord's day. That is why its institutions were conferences and its authorities were personalities, and why, when several of those personalities fell, congregations discovered they had no structure to catch them. A movement gathered around men is only as durable as the men. The older Reformed answer to that is unglamorous and is the point: a confession a church subscribes, a plurality of elders, and a court above the local pulpit.

First Corinthians 3 is the diagnostic text, and it was written about exactly this dynamic. The Corinthians were not heretics; they were enthusiasts who had attached themselves to teachers, and Paul calls the arrangement carnal and then dismantles it: who then is Paul, and who is Apollos, but ministers by whom ye believed? I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase. The cure is not fewer teachers but a right estimate of them, and a man who cannot name his convictions without naming his favourite preacher has the Corinthian problem.

None of that cancels the good, which was considerable. A generation that had been given therapeutic preaching was handed Romans, and found it could bear weight; churches that had chased relevance began to sing about the wrath of God being satisfied. Second Timothy 4:3 describes the age the resurgence pushed against — when they will not endure sound doctrine, but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers — and any movement that made sound doctrine endurable again to young men did a real work, whatever it left undone.
roots_summary: Greek charis (G5485), grace; sarkikos (G4559), carnal, fleshly; diakonos (G1249), minister; hugiaino (G5198), to be sound, healthy, of doctrine.
roots_lines: Greek sarkikos (G4559) — carnal; 1 Corinthians 3:1, 3:3–4, 2 Corinthians 10:4.
Greek diakonos (G1249) — minister, servant; 1 Corinthians 3:5, Ephesians 3:7, Colossians 1:23.
Greek hugiaino (G5198) — to be sound; 2 Timothy 4:3, 1:13, Titus 1:9, 2:1.
usage: “I am of Paul; and another, I am of Apollos” — the movement's diagnostic text.
“I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase” — the right estimate of a teacher.
“They will not endure sound doctrine” — the age it pushed against.
